models.purpose: Give the walking speed in an ordinary channel as a straight line in the crowd density, with one slope per channel type.
models.summary: Predtechenskii and Milinskii fitted a nonlinear speed-density curve from aisle and stair observations. The paper rejects it as too complex and adopts the Nelson-Mowrer linear form v = k - 0.266 k D, valid for 0.54 to 3.8 persons per square metre. D is the share of the channel area taken by bodies. k is read from a table: 1.00 to 1.23 for stairs by riser and tread, 1.40 for corridor, aisle, ramp and doorway. The paper picks k = 1 for the staircase model and k = 1.4 for the corridor model, then says the line fails at high density such as a narrow room exit.

models.purpose: Replace the linear speed law at high density by a speed that depends on crowding from the front, crowding from the side, and the traits of the people.
models.summary: Following Lu Junan, the paper splits crowding into front and side. Front crowding puts a damping force proportional to the relative speed over the gap to the person ahead. Side crowding is a friction term said to matter only at high density. Newton's second law gives equation (2), printed with a minus on the left-hand side, so a positive damping force would speed the person up; the sign fights the prose. One integration gives equation (3). People are placed on a grid of spacing L plus a front gap and a side gap, giving two linear densities. Setting speed to zero at the maximum densities fixes the constant, and the paper says it substitutes an unnamed quantity a into equation (1) to reach the two-regime equation (5), which does not follow from equation (1). Equation (6) drops k and the mass and adds three weights alpha, beta, gamma that are never given values. Body sizes from Roytman and spacing from Ando fix the four densities, and equation (7) states A = 1.32 - 0.82 ln(rho) and B = 3.0 - 0.76 rho with no derivation. Equation (8) writes the speed as v_m times a weighted sum of A, B and gamma. The appendix code never calls this model.

models.purpose: Turn the building into one matrix and recompute the maximum flow from one source to one sink at every time step.
models.summary: The building is split into n rooms and drawn as a graph. Two virtual nodes are added: node 1, a source whose edges carry the people still in each room, and node n+2, a sink fed by the exits. This cuts a many-rooms-to-many-exits problem down to one source and one sink. Four matrices fill an (n+2) by (n+2) frame. The corridor matrix uses the linear speed and is symmetric with a zero diagonal. The staircase matrix uses the SES speed. The initial matrix holds the room counts in its first row. The export matrix holds the exit flows in its last column. Their sum is the overall matrix G. Maximising the escape rate is renamed as the maximum flow from source to sink, found by Ford-Fulkerson; the proof is declined and the max-flow min-cut theorem is cited. Each iteration is one time step. It builds the flow matrix and the margin matrix, updates the room counts, and resets each channel capacity from its new density. It stops when the source holds fewer than 0.5 people. The emergency branch, which blocks entry to a threatened room, is described in prose and commented out in the code.

details: Room counts start as the source edges.
The test building draws room counts at random between 100 and 200 and sets exit capacities at 40, 35 and 30 persons per second.
The source connects only to rooms and the sink only to exits.

steps: Build the graph with the source and the sink.
Find an augmenting path by breadth-first search.
Push flow along it and repeat until no path remains.
Record the flow matrix and the margin matrix for the time step.
Update the room counts from the flow matrix.
Recompute each channel capacity from its new density.
Stop when the source holds fewer than 0.5 people.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Ford-Fulkerson stops when no augmenting path remains. The outer loop stops when the source holds fewer than 0.5 people. The paper notes the inner method can loop forever on some values and judges that chance almost zero for a crowd.

assumptions: Signs are clear and most people follow them.
No stampedes and no counter-flow, though the corridor matrix is symmetric.
Main doors are of moderate size.
One time step can be treated as a steady maximum flow.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The test building of 770 people is reported solved in 0.457 seconds and the Louvre run of 6700 people in 36.15 seconds, giving a total evacuation of 288.7 seconds. The room counts are random and no recorded evacuation is compared, and the code does not run the emergency branch.

validation_refs: Figure 15 sensitivity at five percent density error.
models.computational_cost: 0.457 seconds for 770 people. 36.15 seconds for 6700 people at a 0.1 second step. Storage grows with the precision.
strengths: Replanning each step lets the route follow the density.
The flow matrix and the margin matrix show the bottlenecks directly.
Opening or closing a channel is an edit to the matrix.
limitations: The corridor matrix allows flow both ways while assumption 4 forbids counter-flow.
The prose says six rooms numbered 2 to 7, while Figure 3 shows nodes 2 to 8.
The summary uses 6700 people and section 7.2 says about 7000.
The emergency handling that supports the adaptability claim is commented out in the code.
Ford-Fulkerson non-termination is dismissed as almost zero rather than shown.
